..
Issued at 243 AM CST Mon Nov 2 2026

Today into Tonight... 

Temperatures and humidity will remain above seasonal normals today 
as highs crest to near 80 F near and north of I-20 and into the 
lower 80s F to the south. Dewpoints will generally be in the 60s F 
across the area. The chances for rain sink today with overall fair 
weather expected. We could see the sun peaking through by afternoon 
but mostly cloudy conditions will continue ahead of our next 
potential weather maker late Tuesday. Temperatures tonight will dip 
into the 60s F, held from dipping further by clouds and deep 
boundary layer moisture. 

Tuesday into Wednesday...

Deep return flow between a departing deep layer ridge and incoming 
deep layer trough will continue to advect warm, moist air from the 
south and east through much of Tuesday. In the lower levels, the 
imported airmass will have trajectories of modified continental 
origin, having been dragged across portions of the southwestern 
Atlantic/Gulf Stream and into the Southeastern US. This airmass will 
be marginally unstable (~750-1500 J/KG MUCAPE) but we won't likely 
see air of true Gulf/tropical origin getting into our area until 
boundary layer winds shift more southerly directly ahead of the 
approaching cold front. This likely results in a somewhat pinched 
warm sector that, combined with the likely late day approach of 
stronger frontal forcing after the diurnal instability maximum, will 
substantially limit our local severe weather threat. At the same 
time, the better upper dynamics associated with the upper trough 
could be on a downward trend as the projected 500 mb height center 
fills from near 560 dam to around 546 dam and lifts northward more 
quickly than it can make eastward progress toward the ArkLaMiss. 
This is somewhat offset by the trough orientation becoming more 
neutrally tilted than the positive orientation it will likely 
exhibit to our west. Deep layer effective bulk shear likely rises to 
around 40 kts with 0-1 km helicity anemic, in the sub 100 M^2/S^2 
range for much of the area. The net result, though, still yields 
marginally supportive parameters for an isolated, lower-end severe 
weather risk. A Marginal Risk (1 out of 5) for severe weather 
remains in place for this reason across about the western third of 
the area, generally west of I-55. With limited instability becoming 
even harder to come by late in the day and the forcing for ascent 
being consolidated into a narrow frontal channel, thunderstorms 
likely present linearly in the form of a squall/QLCS. The primary 
severe hazard is then likely to be the threat for damaging wind 
gusts as high as 60 mph though a brief, embedded, weak tornado 
can't be totally ruled out. 

Thunderstorms producing heavy rain is likely in a few areas 
though overall storms appear to be progressive in nature. Still, 
in areas where this brief, heavy rainfall occurs, there could 
exist a risk for localized flash flooding. Central and northern 
portions of the area would likely see the highest risk of isolated
flash flooding. These areas included in the "Limited" risk for 
flash flooding are expected to see between 1 and 2 inches of rain 
with locally higher amounts possible. 

Rain and storms move west to east across the area into Wednesday 
morning, likely exiting the area in most part by noon. Temperatures 
Tuesday and Wednesday will be warm, 70s F and 80s F for highs, 60s 
for lows Tuesday night, before then turning sharply colder after 
frontal passage. 

Wednesday Night into Early Next Week ... 

Surface high pressure builds in behind the front as seasonably cool 
air replaces the moist and warm airmass currently in place. Skies 
likely have time to become mostly clear by Wednesday night and as 
northwesterly winds become lighter, we will radiate effectively 
overnight. This will allow temperatures to drop into the mid/upper 
40s F for most with 50s F hanging on for the southeastern third of 
the area. The airmass incoming isn't of arctic origin, however, and 
the dewpoints quickly rebound into the 50s F on Thursday on westerly 
winds that will have most recently traversed a seasonably very warm 
and moist Southwest and Southern Plains portion of the country. We 
rebound quickly back into the mid/upper 70s F and lower 80s F 
Thursday, only seeing highs dropping into 60s F by early next week 
as a reinforcing cold front likely arrives. Current trends suggest 
this front could arrive without substantial fanfare, likely dry or 
mostly dry (<0.05") across the area. This does suggest, however, 
that there could be some chance for frost in the day 7-8 range in 
some of the typically cooler spots. /86/
